title: Range Queries: Prefix Sums vs Segment Trees vs Fenwick Trees
oneLiner: Why prefix sums stop working once the array changes, and how a segment tree and a Fenwick tree give O(log n) updates and queries, stepped through node by node.
keyTakeaway: Prefix sums: O(1) query, O(n) update, so only for arrays that don't change. Segment tree: every node stores the summary of a range; update and query are O(log n) for any associative operation (sum, min, max, gcd). Fenwick tree: tree[i] covers the i & -i positions ending at i; add climbs with i += i & -i, prefix descends with i -= i & -i, O(log n) each, about ten lines of code, but only for operations you can undo, like sums and counts.
explanation:
A range query asks for a summary of a contiguous slice of an array: the sum, minimum, maximum or count of nums[l..r]. A point update changes one element; a range update changes every element of a slice. Prefix Sums (Patterns track) answers a range sum in O(1) after an O(n) build, but only while the array is fixed: changing nums[i] shifts every prefix after i, so each update costs O(n). The interview follow-up is almost always "now the array also changes". Two structures make both operations O(log n).

Segment tree. A binary tree in which every node covers a range of indices and stores the summary of that range. The root covers [0, n - 1]; a node covering [lo, hi] splits at mid = (lo + hi) / 2 into a left child [lo, mid] and a right child [mid + 1, hi]; each leaf covers one index. It lives in a plain array like a heap: root at 1, node k's children at 2k and 2k + 1, and 4n slots are always enough. Build, O(n): leaves are the elements, each parent combines its two children. Point update, O(log n): walk down to the leaf, change it, recompute each ancestor on the way back up. One node per level. Range query, O(log n): a node completely outside [l, r] returns the identity (the value that changes nothing: 0 for sum, infinity for min); a node completely inside returns its stored value without going deeper; a node that partly overlaps asks both children. At most about four nodes per level are visited. The combine can be anything associative, meaning (a op b) op c = a op (b op c), so the tree's fixed grouping can't change the answer: sum, min, max, gcd, AND, OR, XOR, or even "maximum subarray sum" with a few fields per node. That flexibility is the main reason to choose it.

Fenwick tree, also called a binary indexed tree or BIT. An array tree[1..n], indexed from 1, where tree[i] stores the sum of the lowbit(i) elements ending at position i. lowbit(i) = i & -i is the value of i's lowest set bit (see the Bit Manipulation Toolkit): lowbit(12) = lowbit(1100 in binary) = 4, so tree[12] holds positions 9 to 12. prefix(i), the sum of positions 1..i: add tree[i], then i -= i & -i, until i is 0. Each step clears the lowest set bit, so 13 -> 12 -> 8 -> 0 adds ranges [13], [9..12] and [1..8]. At most log n steps. add(i, delta): add delta to tree[i], then i += i & -i, until i > n. Each step moves to the next cell whose range also covers i: 5 -> 6 -> 8 -> 16. Range sum l..r = prefix(r) - prefix(l - 1). Build with n adds in O(n log n), or in O(n) by adding each tree[i] into its parent tree[i + lowbit(i)]. It is 1-indexed because lowbit(0) = 0, so i += 0 would never move: shift array index i to i + 1. A Fenwick tree is shorter to write than a segment tree, uses n + 1 slots instead of 4n, and runs faster, but a range answer is a difference of two prefixes, so the operation needs an inverse. Sums and counts have one; min and max don't, so range minimum needs a segment tree.

Fenwick trees as counters. Index the tree by value instead of position and store how many times each value has been seen; then prefix(v) is "how many seen values are <= v". That one idea solves Count of Smaller Numbers After Self and Count Inversions. When values are huge or negative, first apply coordinate compression: sort the distinct values and replace each by its rank, 1 to k.

In an interview, the usual expectation is to name the structure, state the costs, and code a Fenwick tree or a recursive segment tree with point updates in about 15 minutes. Lazy propagation, for range updates, is the next lesson.

The widgets: compare total work for a mix of updates and queries, step a segment tree through build, update and query, and step a Fenwick tree through its lowbit jumps.
